primitives.name: Expected Maximum of Two Correlated Gaussians
primitives.verbatim_quote: Method / model For two lineups with score vectors, the paper uses the closed-form expression for E[max] of two correlated Gaussians (from the literature): E[max(X1,X2)] = μ1Φ(δ) + μ2Φ(-δ) + θφ(δ), where δ = (μ1-μ2)/θ, θ = √(σ12 + σ22 - 2σ12), Φ/φ are standard normal CDF/PDF.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'X1, X2': 'random variables representing scores of two lineups (dimensionless)', 'μ1, μ2': 'means of respective lineup scores (points)', 'σ1, σ2': 'standard deviations of respective lineup scores (points)', 'σ12': 'covariance between lineup scores (points²)', 'Φ, φ': 'standard normal CDF and PDF (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Scores are jointly Gaussian; means are unbiased; variances and correlations estimated from historical data.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When σ12 approaches σ1σ2, the formula degenerates into single-Gaussian limit.

layer2.mapping: Maps to GSI’s Bayesian inference of lineup dominance; GSE’s policy gradient over E[max] outcomes.
layer2.telemetry: Expected score difference between top two lineups in simulated contests.

primitives.name: Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming Optimization
primitives.verbatim_quote: They formulate a mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP) maximizing this objective subject to Showdown lineup constraints, and solve it with a cutting-plane algorithm extending the integer L-shaped method — iteratively adding linear cuts that upper-bound the nonlinear objective.
primitives.latex: \max_{x_1, x_2} \mathbb{E}[\max(c^T x_1 \xi, c^T x_2 \xi)] \quad \text{s.t. } x_i \in \{0,1\}^n, \text{ constraints}
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'x1, x2': 'binary lineup vectors (dimensionless)', 'c': 'coefficient vector of projected points (points)', 'ξ': 'multivariate Gaussian random vector of player scores (points)', 'n': 'number of available players (dimensionless)'}
primitives.assumptions: Lineup constraints are deterministic; objective function is concave in x.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When constraint space becomes infeasible or solution space too large for cutting-plane convergence.

layer2.mapping: Derives GSE’s constrained optimization engine for multi-entry portfolios; enables GSI’s robustness checks on lineup selection.
layer2.telemetry: Number of iterations until convergence of cutting-plane algorithm.

primitives.name: Gaussian Multivariate Modeling of Player Scores
primitives.verbatim_quote: Equations & assumptions - Objective: max E[max(cTx1·ξ, cTx2·ξ)] where ξ ~ N(μ, Σ), x1,x2 are binary lineup vectors.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: {'ξ': 'player score vector (points)', 'μ': 'mean score vector (points)', 'Σ': 'covariance matrix of player scores (points²)'}
primitives.assumptions: Player scores follow multivariate normal distribution; mean and covariance are known or estimated.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When player score distributions deviate significantly from normality or when Σ is not positive semi-definite.

layer2.mapping: Enables GSI’s probabilistic forecasting of lineup outcomes; supports GSE’s risk-adjusted lineup generation.
layer2.telemetry: Kullback-Leibler divergence between empirical and modeled score distributions.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that optimizing E[max(X1,X2)] for two correlated lineups under a multivariate Gaussian model provides a principled way to hedge against variance in individual lineup performance. This is mathematically grounded in the closed-form expression for the expected maximum of two correlated Gaussians, derived from properties of the standard normal distribution. The optimization problem is NP-hard, necessitating a mixed-integer nonlinear program (MINLP) solved via cutting-plane methods. The key innovation lies in treating both lineups as jointly distributed under a shared covariance structure, enabling a more nuanced strategy than independent EV maximization. Failure modes include overfitting due to small sample size (16 contests), ad-hoc correlation zeroing, and misestimation of tail dependencies. The method assumes Gaussianity and stationarity of player performance, which may not hold in volatile environments like DFS. The dual nature of the problem—optimizing for both expected value and risk—is captured through the closed-form expression, which inherently balances mean and variance components. This framework directly informs GSI’s Bayesian inference pipeline and GSE’s state-transition logic for lineup selection.
